list.listitem: Since congenital hypothyroidism (CH) is asymptomatic at birth, universal newborn screening has been shown to identify affected children leading to treatment and reduction of the long-term effects of congenital hypothyroidism. A
Screening before 48 hours (term infants) or <7 days (preterm) may result in false positive results. C
If screened positive, treatment (levothyroxine 10-15 mcg/kg/d) should be started urgently as the outcome depends on the timely introduction of treatment. A
The treatment replaces the missing hormone thyroxine. In cases of permanent congenital hypothyroidism (CH), treatment is lifelong. A
With treatment there is no significant reduction in intelligence. B
Careful follow-up is needed as up to one third of patients stop medication before 3 years of age without medical supervision, and it appears from one study that most require lifelong treatment. B

background.definition: Decreased or absent thyroid function and thyroid hormone production, present at birth. Congenital hypothyroidism (CH) may be of thyroidal or central origin.

list.listitem: Twice as common in female infants compared with male infants.
Variations in incidence and prevalence among populations is likely associated with differences in genetic expression and local prevalence of iodine deficiency.
One per 3000 to 4000 births in US and northern European populations.
Higher incidence in some ethnic groups, for example, among the Greek Cypriot population (1 per 1800) and Asian-identifying people in Northern England (1 per 918).

In a New Zealand population study, the overall incidence of central hypothyroidism (CH) rose from 2.6 to 3.6 per 10,000 live births over an 18-year period, thought to be due to a shift in population with proportionately more births to Asian- and Pacific Islander-identifying people.
In a study in the Netherlands, central CH was identified in 1:16 000 neonates; coexisting growth hormones or ACTH deficiency may pose additional risks.

In a Dutch cohort of 1200 children with CH (1995-2011), 143 had central CH and 1057 had thyroidal CH. Four children (2.8%) with central CH and 280 children (26.5%) had severe hypothyroidism based on measured free T4.

In a population screening study in the UK, 730 of 837,377 babies were referred for diagnostic confirmation of CH. There were 134 cases of thyroid ectopia for an incidence of 16 per 100,000 births, and 73 cases of thyroid agenesis.

In California, from 1990 to 1998, a study evaluating prevalence ratios among different ethnic groups demonstrated a prevalence ratio of 0.3 (95% CI, 0.2-0.4) for both White and Black infants, 1.6 (95% CI, 1.4-1.8) among Hispanic infants, and 2.9 (95% CI, 1.9-4.4), among Asian infants.
CH is one of the most common preventable causes of developmental delay.

Children with CH have a higher prevalence of hearing loss (pooled prevalence 16.1%, 95% confidence interval [CI] 10.7, 22.4). In these children, there is evidence of subclinical abnormalities of the cochlea and eighth cranial nerve despite early initiation of levothyroxine therapy.
Most cases are due to thyroid dysgenesis, a defect in thyroid hormone synthesis, or resistance to thyroid hormone.

Thyroid dysgenesis (80-85%) is due to failure of thyroid to migrate at the correct anatomical site. This abnormal organogenesis can cause thyroid agenesis, hypoplastic, or ectopic gland. It is associated with PAX8, NKX2X, FOXE1, NKX-2, and HHEX genes.
Thyroid hormone synthesis defects account for 10-15%. Affected genes include DUOX2, DUOXA2, TPO, TG, SLC26A4, SLC5A5, and TSHR.
Resistance to thyroid hormone (<5%), is due to decrease in sensitivity of target tissue to thyroid hormone. It is associated with SLC2GA2, THRA, or THRB gene.
Antithyroid drugs taken during pregnancy, prematurity, iodine deficiency or excess, or heterozygous dyshormogenesis.

However, authors of a meta-analysis of 13 randomized controlled trials and cohort studies involving 18,948 infants found no significant association between maternal treatment with propylthiouracil for hyperthyroidism in pregnancy and the control group for either congenital anomalies or neonatal hypothyroidism (OR 0.55, 95%CI 0.06-4.92, I2 = 57.0%).
In premature babies, 40% of 23-week and 10% of 28-week premature infants had severely reduced T4 value (<4 mg/dL).
Cause remains unknown in about 20% of transient cases.
CH results from disruption of normal thyroid function at one of several stages.

Most commonly hypothyroidism is due to problems with formation of the thyroid gland tissue. The thyroid gland is formed between the 4th and 10th weeks of gestation. It arises from the fourth brachial pouch and migrates to the front of the neck. Any disruption to this process can lead to thyroid dysgenesis and result in gland dysfunction.
In a minority of cases, thyroid anatomy is normal but there is a problem with production, release, or end-organ response to thyroid hormones.
The thyroid gland produces tetraiodothyronine and triiodothyronine. The synthesis of these hormones is controlled by the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis.

All 50 states and the District of Columbia require newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism. Blood spot thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) or thyroxine (T4) can be used, ideally between 2 and 4 days of life. Universal screening prevents long-term harms from congential hypothyroidism. A
Screening before 48 hours (term infants) or 7 days (preterm) can result in false positive results. C

Consider a second screening for preterm neonates, low-birth-weight and very low-birth-weight neonates, ill and preterm newborns admitted to neonatal intensive care units, multiple births, and when specimen collection occurred within the first 24 hours of life. C
A positive screening result should prompt a referral for confirmatory testing within 24 hours. A

Universal screening can prevent negative low-term outcomes from CH. Most neonates with congenital hypothroidism (CH) have no signs or symptoms at birth. Therefore, all 50 states and the District of Columbia require newborn screening for congenital hypothyroidism.
Blood spot thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) or thyroxine (T4) can be used.
Screening using TSH levels misses 5% of CH that is not primary compared to T4 screen.
The European Society for Paediatric Endocrinology (ESPE, 2020-2021) consensus guideline recommends TSH as the most sensitive screening test.

TSH screening cutoff levels vary; in the US screening cutoffs of 15-30 mU/L are used for the first test and 5-15 mU/L for the second test. Lowering cutoff levels results in higher detection rates of primarily functional disorders of unknown importance. In one retrospective study, lowering the TSH cutoff rate from 15 mU/l to 10 mU/L led to no significant change in detection of cases of permanent CH but an 8-fold increase in detection of transient CH.

In a screening study of infants in Scotland, optimal capillary TSH threshold for predicting a venous free T4 of <10 pmol/L was >40 mU/L (90.3% sensitivity and 65.9% specificity). Among infants whose capillary TSH was ≤40 mU/L, 7 cases of CH were confirmed on subsequent testing.

There are also differences by ethnicity, possibly reflecting differences in genetic expression or maternal thryoid disease, in exceeding any TSH cutoff level (4-10 mU/L) with the odds ratio (OR) Chinese infants having the highest OR for congenital hypothyroidism in one study.
One approach is to perform TSH and T4 simultaneously. This will allow detection of central CH.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) recommends that "blood be collected when the infant is between 2 and 4 days of age" ESPE states that "the best 'window' for testing is from 48 to 72 hours of age"
Screening before 48 hours (term infants) or 7 days (preterm) can result in false positive results.
Infants that are small for gestational age (SGA) may have a higher risk of false negative response due to a physiologic delay in TSH response postnatally.

Screening using both TSH and T4 should be considered for children with Down syndrome; in one study, total T4 concentrations did not correlate with screening TSH concentrations and only 10 or 20 infants with CH and Down syndrome were identified via T4-based screening.
The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends screening children with Down syndrome at birth, 6 months, and 12 months of age.

ESPE recommends consideration of a second screening for preterm neonates, low-birth-weight and very low-birth-weight neonates, ill and preterm newborns admitted to neonatal intensive care units, multiple births, and when specimen collection occurred within the first 24 hours of life. Second screening should be considered at approximately 10-14 days of age. For infants with Down syndrome, a second screening is recommended at the end of the neonatal period (28 days old).
Preterm babies( < 32 weeks), and very low birth weight (VLBW) infants are at risk of transient low T4 of prematurity or delayed TSH rise, should be re-tested at 2-4 weeks later.

In a cohort study conducted over 13 years using TSH screening collected between 72 and 120 hours after birth with repeat samples collected weekly in preterm infants until the infant was term-corrected (37 weeks' gestation), CH was diagnosed after the initial screen in 27 (50.9%) infants, 6 of whom had permanent CH and 4 of whom had severe CH.

If repeat screening is planned for preterm infants, appropriate cutoff values may need to be adjusted based on gestational age at birth. In a cohort study in Wisconsin, at 3-4 weeks after birth the 95th percentile TSH level range was 11 to 11.8 μIU/mL for the group born at 22 to 27 weeks' gestation and 8.2 to 9 μIU/mL for the group born at 28 to 31 weeks' gestation. For the earlier birth group, the TSH nadir was reached at 11-12 weeks of life compared to 5-6 weeks for the latter birth group.
Because the outcome depends on early treatment, a positive screening result should prompt a referral for confirmatory testing within 24 hours.
Most cases of CH are not preventable. Maternal exposure to radioactive iodine and iodine-based antiseptics should be avoided.

Confirm screening result with formal thyroid function testing immediately, ideally within 24 hours of a positive screening test result. If the TSH is >40mU/L, treatment should be started without waiting for additional diagnostic evaluation. C
See for management of an abnormal screening result. C
Thyroid imaging with radionuclide scan and/or ultrasound will identify thyroid dysgenesis if present (accounts for 85% of cases). C

Differential.Differential_Features: Low TSH and T4 + other hormone deficiencies; abnormal pituitary MRI findings
Hypoglycemia due to hyperinsulinism, macrosomia, omphalocele, fissured earlobes
Constipation only; absent ganglion cells on rectal biopsy, normal thyroid function

list.listitem: Maternal history of autoimmune thyroid disease, antithyroid medication, and exposure to excessive iodine can suggest antenatally that there may be increased risk of congenital hypothyroidism (CH) in the newborn.
In areas of iodine deficiency and where dietary supplementation (eg, salt iodination) is inadequate, endemic goiter is still a significant cause of CH.
The majority of patients with CH are detected by screening before they become symptomatic.

Clinical features develop with time and may include feeding difficulties, lethargy, constipation, hypotonia, bradycardia, prolonged jaundice, umbilical hernia, low temperature, macroglossia and hoarse cry.
The above should prompt consideration of CH, particularly where screening is not in place, and where screening only measures TSH.

TSH versus T4 assays for screening produce similar results. National screening guidelines usually quote around 95% sensitivity and 99.9% specificity. In one study where cases missed by screening were actively sought, TSH-based screening was 96.8% sensitive (95% CI, 87.8-99.4) and 99.9% specific (99.9-99.9).

In another study of 4 different screening protocols over 4 time periods, TSH testing with serial testing for children with birth weights <1800 g outperformed thyroxine (T4), tandem T4 and TSH (highest sensitivity but higher false-positive rate), and TSH without serial follow-up. Two children of normal birthweight later admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit were missed despite screening.

Radionuclide scintigraphy is considered the 'gold standard' for visualizing ectopic thyroid tissue. In one study of 174 screening-referred infants with 151 having normally-located thyroid on scintigraphy, ultrasound was found to be 95.8% sensitive (95% CI, 76.8-99.7) and 99.3% specific (95.8-100) for absence of normal thyroid. In another study of 40 infants, ultrasound failed to detect all 11 ectopic thyroids, but did confirm normal thyroid location in 6 cases with no isotope uptake. Combined imaging gives more diagnostic information, although ultrasound could be considered the initial diagnostic modality to reduce radiation exposure and cost.

The AAP and the ESPE (2020-2021) recommend either scintigraphy or ultrasound imaging to assess cause and severity; both should be considered in infants with a high TSH. Intrauterine testing can be considered using knee X-ray looking for presence or absence of femoral and tibial epiphyses. ESPE strongly recommends starting levothyroxine treatment before conducting thyroid gland imaging studies. An initial TSH/freeT4 ratio > 4.8 after first laboratory evaluation, was found to predict transient elevated TSH/ low T4 with 90% sensitivity and 91% specificity (AUC 0.947, p=0.0001). If the initial ratio > 12.5, it predicted CH with 100% sensitivity and 99% specificity (AUC 0.999, p=0.0001)

list.listitem: Screening tests for hearing should be conducted during infancy and before school age. B
ESPE (2020-2021) guidelines recommend that neonates with high TSH concentrations should be examined for congenital malformations (particularly cardiac) and for dysmorphic features.

ESPE (2020-2021) guidelines recommend targeted genetic counseling for infants or children with CH and associated disorders (e.g., congenital heart disease, kidney malformations). Patients with thyroid dyshormonogenesis or familial occurrence of dysgenesis and central hypothyroidism should be considered for further genetic testing. B
Treatment should be started as soon as possible after congenital hypothyroidism (CH) is confirmed by serum thyroid function tests to ensure best neurodevelopmental outcome. A

The AAP and the ESPE (2020-2021) recommend immediate initiation of treatment if the TSH is >40 mU/L in whole blood without waiting for confirmatory test results unless they are available on the same day. B Immediate treatment is also recommended if the free T4 (fT4) concentration is below normal for age. A
The recommended starting dose of levothyroxine is 10 to 15 mcg/kg/d. A
If CH is suspected, the treatment is urgent; a delay may result in irreversible CNS damage leading to developmental delay.

Replacement therapy with levothyroxine sodium is the treatment of choice. The starting dose of levothyroxine for a neonate is 10 to 15 mcg/kg once daily. Crushed tablets in water or breast milk can be administered orally with a small spoon. ESPE prefers use of brand name rather than generic products. For patients with milder forms of central CH, EPSE, 2020-2021, suggests starting treatment at a lower dose of 5–10 μg/kg/day to avoid the risk of overtreatment which can also affect neurodevelopmental outcomes.

In an open RCT with 72 Italian children with CH, there were no differences in growth or neurobehavioral development at 24 months and 4 years comparing initial levothyroxine dosing at 10-12.5 μg/kg/day vs. 12.6-15 μg/kg/day. At 4 years, 24 children in the low-dose and 21 children in the higher dose arms were available for follow-up.
For children with CH, levothyroxine as liquid solution formulation was noninferior to levothyroxine tablets, with less need for dose adjustment at 6 months, based on an RCT with 39 children with CH.

The dose is adjusted depending on T4 and TSH levels, which should be checked 2 and 4 weeks after starting thyroxine, testing at least 4 hours after the last dose. In infants with normalization of TSH, monitoring should continue every 1 to 3 months in the first year of life. The aim is to keep the level of T4 in the first year of life between 10 and 16 mcg/dL.
Avoid concomitant use of soy formula, fiber, or iron. Breastfeeding can continue.

The AAP and ESPE (2020-2021) recommend that TSH concentration be maintained in the age-specific reference range and T4 in the upper half of the age-specific range. ESPE notes that if TSH is in the age-specific reference interval, fT4 concentrations above the upper limit of the reference interval can be accepted; reduction of the levothyroxine dose should not be based on a single higher than normal fT4 concentration, unless TSH is suppressed.
In patients with CH and central resistance to thyroid hormone, the addition of liothyronine to levothyroxine monotherapy facilitated normalization of TSH and T4.
In one follow-up study, overtreatment in the first two years with levothyroxine, as measured by fT4 above the age-specific range, resulted in lower IQ scores.
Whether or not premature infants with hypothyroxinemia should be treated remains controversial.

Screening programs have identified a group of children with elevated TSH and normal T4. There have been no long-term studies to evaluate cognitive development in this group of patients although one study found increased frequency of minor morphological, genetic and biochemical abnormalities. Most clinicians recommend treatment to normalize TSH levels. ESPE (2020-2021) recommends treatment if the TSH is above 20 mU/L. For children with normal T4 and TSH between 6 and 20 mU/L, they recommend either treatment or diagnostic testing for cause and consideration of immediate treatment or retesting in 2 weeks.
If no cause of permanent hypothyroidism was identified in the neonatal period, the need for treatment should be reviewed after the age of 3 years.
Despite this recommendation, a study using Commercial Claims and Multi-State Medicaid databases found that over a third (38%) of children had discontinued use of thyroid replacement by age 36 months.
Early thyroxine replacement can eliminate the severe neurodevelopmental delay associated with congenital hypothyroidsm (CH) in the pre-screening era. A

Despite screening, data from 4 population-based studies in high-income countries found intellectual disability (defined as an IQ <70) present in 8% to 28% of children with clinically-diagnosed CH. C Recent studies suggest that cohorts treated with currently recommended doses have no significant reduction in IQ. B
In the Italian cohort of children with CH who were treated with 10-15 μg/kg/day, 6 of 45 children followed for 4 years (13.3%) had an IQ below 85 (73.7 ± 5.9) and only 1 child had an IQ below 70.

In a cohort study of cases of CH detected by newborn screening over a 4-year period in Michigan who were followed up after age 3 years (84 cases or about 55% of the original cohort), 34 cases were considered permanent CH, 25% of followed cases with CH were no longer being treated, most (over 83%) had stopped treatment without medical supervision. Of 23 cases that underwent a medically-supervised trial without thyroid hormone medication, treatment was reinstated in 20. C

In one small case series, males (OR 4.85; 95% CI, 1.53-15.37) and those with older mothers (31.5 ± 5.48 years vs 26 ± 6.76 years), delivered by cesarean section (86.7% vs 54.2%) and who had retinopathy of prematurity (37.5% vs 8%) were more likely to have transient vs. permanent CH. C
Transient hypothyroxinemia of prematurity does not influence IQ or motor function based on 19-year follow-up of the Project On Preterm and Small-for-gestational-age birth cohort. C
Concerns regarding subtle behavioral problems due to higher dose treatment have not been consistently confirmed. B

Based on a French survey, fecundity does not appear adversely affected in young adults (women and men) with CH treated early compared to the general population with the exception of women suffering from the most severe form of the disease.C

Women with CH have a higher risk of gestational hypertension, emergency cesarean delivery, induced labor for vaginal delivery, and prematurity compared to a reference sample. In a prospective population with CH, adjusted odds ratios (aOR) (95% confidence interval [CI]) were 2.19 (1.26-3.81), 1.88 (1.17-3.02), 1.58 (1.12-2.24), and 1.85 (1.06-3.25), respectively.

In women with CH who are planning pregnancy, ESPE, 2020-2021, recommends optimization of levothyroxine treatment aiming at TSH concentrations <2.5 mU/L throughout gestation; in addition, these women should be counseled regarding the higher need for LT4 during pregnancy. Free T4 (or total T4) and TSH levels should be monitored every 4 to 6 weeks during pregnancy. Pregnant patients should ingest about 250 μg iodine per day.
After delivery, ESPE recommends lowering levothyroxine to the preconception dose with additional thyroid function testing performed at 6 weeks postpartum.
